title: Rate limiter class design
idea: The rate limiter design is one small `RateLimiter` interface returning a `Decision`, with each algorithm as its own class and time supplied by an injected `Clock`.

analogy.text: A wall socket and the appliances you plug in. The socket shape stays fixed; a kettle or a lamp behaves differently behind it.
analogy.breaks: Appliances draw power; limiters also keep per-key memory between calls.

points: Callers depend only on `RateLimiter` and its single `tryAcquire(key)` method.
A `Decision` record carries allowed, remaining calls, and a retry-after hint.
A `LimitRule` holds the limit and window, and rejects invalid values.
Every algorithm reads time from `Clock`, so tests control time exactly.

edges.label: returns
edges.caption: Every check returns a Decision. The caller never sees counters or buckets.

edges.label: is-a
edges.caption: Token bucket refills a budget at a steady rate and allows short bursts.

edges.label: is-a
edges.caption: Fixed window counts calls in aligned slots, such as each whole second.

edges.label: is-a
edges.caption: Sliding log keeps each call's time and counts those inside the last window.

edges.label: is-a
edges.caption: Sliding counter blends the current and previous window counts to save memory.

edges.label: has 1
edges.caption: Window limiters get one immutable LimitRule; the token bucket takes capacity and refill rate.

edges.label: uses
edges.caption: Limiters ask the injected Clock for time. Production passes the system clock; tests pass a manual one.

code.title: Interfaces and one limiter
code.caption: The types every page builds on, with the simplest algorithm plugged in and a manual clock driving time. Unlike the scope page, `LimitRule` keeps the window in milliseconds and drops `keyType`: the caller picks the key.

walk.text: Three calls per 1000 ms window, with a clock the demo moves by hand.
Four calls from k1, then one from k2, all at time zero.
Move time to the next window and call k1 again.
Clock is one method. ManualClock returns whatever time the test sets.
Decision has two factory methods, so callers never build a half-valid one.
Find the window start, and reset the count when a new window begins.
Under the limit: count and allow. Otherwise reject until the window ends.

pitfalls: Do not call `System.currentTimeMillis` inside a limiter; inject a `Clock` instead.
Do not return a bare boolean; callers need remaining calls and retry-after.
This `HashMap` version is single-threaded; the concurrency page fixes that.

quiz.q: What does the fourth line of ClassDesign print?
quiz.why: The rule allows three calls per window. The fourth k1 call at time 0 is rejected, and the window ends 1000 ms later.

takeaway: One interface, one Decision, one injected Clock; algorithms plug in behind them.

starters: Why is Clock my own interface instead of java.time.Clock?
Should tryAcquire accept a cost for expensive requests?
Where do per-key states live in this design?
